title: Guided practice A: seasonal patterns
subject: science
phenomenonOrContext: Three years of monthly high temperatures at one town repeat the same yearly shape without repeating exactly, and a town in the southern half of Earth records the opposite pattern in the very same months.
lessonGoal: Use several years of weather records to describe a typical season, and name the place that pattern belongs to.
successCriteria: I read every year in the table before I describe a typical season.
I use the word about with a typical temperature, because the years are not identical.
I name the place a seasonal pattern came from instead of claiming it fits everywhere.

vocabulary.definition: a part of the year that has its own usual weather
what usually happens, found by looking at many records
weather that someone measured and wrote down
one half of Earth, either the north half or the south half

sections.title: NOTICE — Three years of highs at Riverbend
sections.body: Riverbend is an example town. Someone there wrote down the average high temperature for four months, three years in a row. Read down a year column first. Then read across a month row and compare the three numbers.

data.tableLabel: Average monthly high temperature at Riverbend, three years of instructional records
data.note: Each number is the average high for that whole month. These records are an instructional example written for this lesson, not published measurements.

sections.title: NOTICE — What repeats and what changes
sections.directions: Use all three year columns. Choose the statement that is true for every row in the table.

items.prompt: Which statement describes the Riverbend records best?

choices.label: July is the warmest month in all three years, and the three July numbers are close but not the same.
July is exactly 83 degrees at Riverbend every year.
The numbers change from year to year, so Riverbend has no yearly pattern.

sections.title: FEEDBACK — A pattern can repeat without repeating exactly
sections.body: Look straight across the July row: 83, then 86, then 81. Those numbers are close to each other, and July is the warmest month in every one of the three years. That is a repeating pattern. Answering exactly 83 every year throws away the 86 and the 81. Answering that there is no pattern throws away the part that did repeat, which is that July was warmest all three times. Weather patterns repeat closely, not perfectly.

sections.title: LEARN — What the word typical means
sections.body: A season is a part of the year with its own usual weather. To describe a season, you need more than one year of records. Any single year can be strange. One hot July on its own does not tell you much. Three hot Julys in a row tell you that hot Julys are typical at that place. Typical means what usually happens, not what happens every single time. That is exactly why scientists put the word about in front of a typical temperature. The word about is honest. It says the years were close to this number without promising that the next year will land on it.

sections.title: MODEL — How I describe a typical July
sections.body: Watch every step I take with the Riverbend table. I am describing a typical July. You will use these same steps on a different month in a moment.

items.prompt: Model task: describe a typical July high at Riverbend.

steps: I find the July row and I read all three numbers, not just one: 83, 86, and 81.
I check whether they are close. The lowest is 81 and the highest is 86, so all three sit within 5 degrees of each other. They are close.
I choose a number near the middle of the three. About 83 degrees is near all three of them.
I write the answer with the word about: a typical July high at Riverbend is about 83 degrees.
I name my evidence out loud: three Julys, 2023, 2024, and 2025, all in the low to middle 80s.
I stop short of promising 83 degrees next July, because not one of these years matched another year exactly.

sections.title: YOUR TURN — A typical January at Riverbend
sections.directions: Use the January row of the Riverbend table: 31, 28, and 34. Take the same steps I took for July.

items.prompt: About what temperature is a typical January high at Riverbend? Enter one number of degrees Fahrenheit.
Which years did you use to get that number, and why is about the right word to put in front of it?

sections.title: FEEDBACK — Check your typical number
sections.body: A good number sits near the middle of 31, 28, and 34. About 31 degrees is near all three. If you wrote 34, you used the warmest January and left the other two out. If you wrote 28, you used the coldest January and left the other two out. One January is not the typical January. The middle of the three is much closer to what usually happens there.

sections.title: FEEDBACK — Name your years and keep the word about
sections.body: A strong answer names all three Januarys, 2023, 2024, and 2025, and says that they came out close but not the same. If your answer leaned on one year, go back and add the other two. If your answer promised an exact temperature for next January, change it to about. You are not being vague when you say about. You are saying exactly as much as three years of records let you say.

sections.title: APPLY — The same July in two places
sections.body: Southpoint is an example town in the southern half of Earth. Riverbend is in the northern half. Both towns measured the same two months of the same year. Riverbend's numbers here are the ones you already used from the 2025 column.

data.tableLabel: Average monthly high temperature at Riverbend and Southpoint in 2025, instructional records
data.note: Both towns recorded the same two months in the same year. These records are an instructional example written for this lesson, not published measurements.

items.prompt: The two towns measured the same two months. What do these records show?

choices.label: When Riverbend is in its warm season, Southpoint is in its cool season.
Both towns are warm in July, because July is summer everywhere on Earth.
Southpoint recorded its months wrong, because July has to be the warmest month.

items.prompt: A student says seasons happen because Earth moves closer to the Sun in summer. Riverbend and Southpoint were both on Earth in the same July. Use the two July numbers to explain why that student's reason cannot be right.

sections.title: FEEDBACK — One Earth, two seasons, the same month
sections.body: In that July, Riverbend was 81 degrees and Southpoint was 48 degrees. Both towns sat on the same Earth in the same month, so Earth was one single distance from the Sun the whole time. One distance cannot make one town warm and the other town cool at once. That rules the student's reason out. Notice what you just did: you did not need to already know the real cause of seasons to show that this cause does not work. Ruling an idea out with evidence is real science, and you will meet the actual cause in a later grade.

sections.title: WHAT YOU LEARNED
sections.body: A season has typical weather, and you find it by comparing several years of records instead of trusting one year. Typical means what usually happens, which is why a careful answer says about. A seasonal pattern also belongs to a place. In the very same month, the northern half and the southern half of Earth are in opposite seasons.

sections.title: EVIDENCE YOU USED
sections.body: You used three years of monthly highs at Riverbend, leaning on the July row and the January row. You used a second table that set Riverbend beside Southpoint in the same two months of 2025. You used the units, degrees Fahrenheit, and the note that both towns recorded the same months.

sections.title: HOW YOU DID
sections.body: Your saved responses hold the typical January number you chose, the years you named as evidence, and your explanation of the two-town record. They stay pending assessment until an approved assessor reviews them. Watching the model July worked out for you does not by itself show that you can do it.

sections.title: WHAT TO PRACTICE
sections.body: Practice two moves. First, read every year in a table before you give a typical value, and keep the word about attached to it. Second, before you use a seasonal pattern anywhere, name the place the records came from.

items.prompt: In one or two sentences, why do three years of January records describe a typical January better than one year of records does?
